chapter_theme: A single song at Vijayamangalam (விஜயமங்கலம்) in Kongu: a frank picture of lovemaking, ending not in a plea but in a vow never to forget Murugan's feet even while serving women.

936.reading: The poet describes lovemaking with a woman whose eyes redden in love's quarrel, whose garlands slip, whose voice hums like a bee, whose breasts bear nail marks and whose lips flow with honeyed nectar, until his life sinks into her navel; he says that even if he melts and becomes the servant of women doing their bidding, he will not forget Murugan's feet from now on. The praise names him nephew of the discus-bearing Narayana who lived as a child in the cowherds' village, son of the skull-bearing lord of ghosts with serpent bracelets, the lord of Vayalur who threw his vel when the hunters cried out and told the Kura girl to stop grieving, and the lord of Vijayamangalam, where bees sing the desi melody over lotus pools.
936.nuance: The turn is unusual: மங்கையர்க்கு ஆளாகி ஏவல் செய்திடினும் நின் கழல் சீர்பாதம் நான் இனி மறவேனே makes no request to be freed from women, only a vow that service to them will not erase the feet. The lines on Vishnu (உலக கண்டமிட்டு ஆகாச மேல் விரி சலதி கண்டிட சேராய மாமவருடன் மடிந்திட) are hard to divide, and the hunters' cry and Valli's grief seem to point to the battle at Valli's hill without naming it.

links.note: Both songs end their account of women not with a plea for release but with a vow: even serving women (மங்கையர்க்கு ஆளாகி ஏவல் செய்திடினும்) in 936, even sinking into courtesans' beds (பாயலின் மூழ்கினும்) in 944, the poet will not forget the feet (மறவேனே). The pair shows a distinct form of the confession, one that keeps devotion beside the habit rather than asking to be freed from it.
